newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine stocks stretch gains at close.
newsitem.headline: Argentine stocks stretch gains at close.

text.p: Argentina's bolsa pushed higher Monday to close September with blue-chip gains of nearly 10 percent.
The MerVal index rose 0.6 percent to 558.86.
"The market is firm but selective, and most investors are now looking forward to tomorrow's global bond launch," said dealer Emilio Alessandro of brokers Alessandro.

A successful placement of Argentina's 10-year bond, expected to be priced at 435-450 basis points over the 10-year U.S. Treasury note, could underpin the market and help offset a rise in the U.S. long bond yield, the dealer said.

"This could be a difficult week for the markets in New York in the run-up to Friday's U.S. jobs report, and since bolsa volumes are very thin we could use the global bond news to offset any turbulence," said Alessandro.

Traders said Wall Street might fare better than U.S. treasuries if the jobs data is too strong, which might help underpin the bolsa and spur a switch from Argentine bonds to stocks. Equities in recent weeks have lagged the fixed income market.
In the session the broad market edged up 0.2 percent, with winners beating losers 25 to 10 and 62 issues unchanged.

Floor volume picked up slightly to 11.8 million pesos from 11.6 million Friday, while over-the-counter deals shrank dramatically to 53.8 million pesos from 180 million Friday. Traders said OTC volume had swelled Friday on end-of-month position squaring.

Best main-tier performers were carmaker Ciadea, which gained 2.2 percent, textile firm and shoemaker Alpargatas and steelmaker Siderca, both up 2.2 percent, and construction stock Polledo, up 2.0 percent.

The heaviest loser was pulp and paper maker Celulosa, which dropped 1.4 percent, followed by food giant Molinos, carmaker Sevel and oil giant YPF, off 0.6 percent, 0.5 percent and 0.2 percent, respectively.

Pepsi bottler Baesa, a second-line stock, tumbled 15 percent. Baesa went unquoted Friday when its ADR nosedived in New York on PepsiCo's admission that it had overextended its operations in Brazil, where it said it had invested "too much, too fast."
